root.note: Probably through a Gallo-Roman phrase *hortus gardinus, ‘a garden closed by a fence’. That phrase is reconstructed.

history: A jardin was defined by its fence. The Franks, the Germanic people who gave France its name, brought a word *gardo or *gart, ‘enclosure’, related to Old High German garto and modern German Garten. The TLFi suggests that people in Gaul spoke of a hortus gardinus, Latin hortus, ‘garden’, with an adjective made from the Frankish word: ‘the fenced garden’. As with fromage, the adjective did the work and the noun disappeared. Medieval Latin has gardinium in the 9th century, and French jardin is attested in the 12th. English borrowed the word from the Anglo-Norman form gardin: that is garden. English yard comes from the same Germanic root, inherited directly, without a trip through France.
historyEinfach: Jardin comes from Frankish, the language of the Franks. Their word gart meant ‘a place with a fence around it’. German Garten is related. English took the word from French: garden. A garden was a piece of land with a fence.

elsewhere.text: English garden came from the Norman French of England. Yard is the same Germanic word, inherited by English without the French detour.
